extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers, essayists, journalists, and advertisers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on plain, effective prose and rhetoric: favors economy, intelligibility, and appropriate register while warning against affected obscurity, excessive ornament, and abusive advertising tactics. Includes examples and anti-patterns drawn from essays and advertisements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to be understood, not to be admired
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man speaks and writes with intent to be understood; one who seeks to be admired transfers his consideration from words to sounds and from sentences to periods, becoming more elegant but less intelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize intelligibility over stylistic showmanship; avoid contriving sentences primarily to impress readers at the expense of conveying meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of expression (shortest route to truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'right' action or opinion effects the design by the fewest means; to find the nearest way from truth to truth, do not use more instruments where fewer will suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor the simplest, most direct phrasing and structure that accomplishes your purpose; do not multiply devices, metaphors, or rhetorical contrivances unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid novelty-for-novelty's-sake
rubrics_metrics.description: Doing common things in an uncommon manner (seeking newness merely because the straight was found out before) is not the character of genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not abandon clear, established methods simply to appear original; novelty must serve clarity or insight, not replace them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exuberance and copiousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The man of exuberance diffuses every thought through many diversities of expression so that it is lost like water in a mist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curb excessive repetition and multiplicity of expression; concentrate and consolidate thoughts so meaning remains vivid and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ponderous, lumped sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: The ponderous dictator of sentences delivers notions in the lump, like uncoined bullion—of more weight than use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break large, dense propositions into clear, usable parts; weighty wording that buries the idea diminishes utility and reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary illustration
rubrics_metrics.description: The liberal illustrator shows by examples and comparisons what was clearly seen when first proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only add examples or comparisons that clarify or illuminate; do not pad clear points with gratuitous illustration that distracts rather than aids understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive formal demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: The stately son of demonstration proves with mathematical formality what no man has yet pretended to doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve rigorous formal proofs for claims that require them; do not over-formalize self-evident truths or common-sense points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the 'bugbear' (terrifick/repulsive) style that obscures truth
rubrics_metrics.description: A style by which evident truths are so obscured they can no longer be perceived: 'terrifick', 'repulsive', or the 'bugbear style'—more terror than danger and repels the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using obscure jargon, scholastic subtleties, or masquerading language that disguises plain propositions; prefer plain English so truths remain accessible (illustrated by the 'Letters concerning Mind' example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid scholastic jargon that frightens rather than informs
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract scholastic phrasing (e.g., elaborate redefinition of 'are') can present nothing new yet intimidate the reader with strange sounds and needless technicality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introducing technical terms or abstract distinctions, ensure they genuinely add clarity; otherwise use familiar language and concrete examples (two and two still make four).

rubrics_metrics.name: Match register and complexity to audience and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Facility and usefulness often coincide; parts of knowledge that are generally necessary are easy; refinements cater to curiosity or idleness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a level of detail, technicality, and ornament appropriate to your readers' needs—avoid over-specializing when communicating general or practical matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: In advertising, promise boldly but responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Promise, large promise, is the soul of an advertisement—advertisers use magnificent promises to gain attention (wash-ball and duvet examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use striking claims to attract readers, but ensure claims are credible; avoid extravagant falsehoods that undermine trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: In advertising, modest sincerity is persuasive
rubrics_metrics.description: Some advertisers know the prejudice of mankind in favour of modest sincerity (example: beautifying fluid that modestly admits limits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admit realistic limitations where appropriate; candid, measured claims can be more convincing than grandiose but implausible ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not censure competitors in ads; promote yourself, not denigrate others
rubrics_metrics.description: In an advertisement it is allowed to speak well of oneself, but one ought not to exclude others from the same pretensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus advertising on your product's merits rather than attacking rivals; unnecessary asperity injures discourse and may repel discerning readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind association and posterity in public writing
rubrics_metrics.description: An advertiser should write with consciousness of a character that will stand among eminent names in the paper; regard is to be paid to posterity—papers may be collected and read later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the company your copy keeps and how it will be perceived over time; craft language worthy of lasting record and appropriate associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid improper juxtaposition of subjects in publications
rubrics_metrics.description: The improper disposition of advertisements can make the noblest objects ridiculous (camel/dromedary followed by Dublin butter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to layout and adjacent content when placing or composing material; context can amplify or deform a message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid playing wantonly with readers' passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers sometimes play too wantonly with our passions (registrar of lottery-tickets, anodyne necklace preying on maternal fear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not deliberately manipulate strong emotions (fear, grief, parental anxiety) in a way that exploits rather than informs or helps the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value simplicity and usefulness over refined ostentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout natural and moral life, necessaries are like iron (common, useful) and superfluities like gold (rare, decorative); refinements are often luxury produced by plenty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor practical clarity and usefulness in content; ornamental refinements should be consciously chosen and not confuse essential meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consolatory/religious discourse when appropriate to comfort, not abstract philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion can give patience and real alleviation of loss where speculative philosophy may only silence or stiffen the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing grief or existential concerns in writing intended to console, consider approaches that offer comfort and hope rather than abstract technical argumentation that may not soothe readers.
